sources.title: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight
sources.keyFinding: Five hazards: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, hostile closed environments; they compound one another.

sources.title: Risks of Human Spaceflight
sources.keyFinding: Lists specific risks including behavioral changes, inadequate sleep, SANS, immune changes and radiation-induced cancer.

sources.title: Radiation Protection technical brief (NASA-STD-3001)
sources.keyFinding: Career limit 600 mSv for all astronauts; 250 mSv short-term limit per solar particle event.

sources.title: Carbon Dioxide technical brief OCHMO-TB-004
sources.keyFinding: 1-hour average CO2 limited to 3 mmHg; headaches reported between 2.8 and 4.5 mmHg.

sources.title: Prevalence of sleep deficiency and use of hypnotic drugs in astronauts before, during, and after spaceflight: an observational study
sources.keyFinding: Wrist actigraphy showed about 6 hours of sleep a night in flight (ISS 6.09 h, shuttle 5.96 h), although NASA rules set aside 8.5 hours for sleep.

sources.title: Impact of Sleep Shifting Strategies on the ISS
sources.keyFinding: Crews have historically averaged around six hours of sleep per night.

sources.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of bone loss in space travelers
sources.keyFinding: Cites a long-known loss rate of 1 to 1.5% a month; measured about 0.8% a month in the lower limbs.

sources.title: Astronaut exercise research on the station
sources.keyFinding: Exercise is the main countermeasure against bone and muscle loss; crew members average about two hours of exercise a day.

sources.title: An Evidence-Based Approach To Exercise Prescriptions on ISS
sources.keyFinding: Station exercise is scheduled at 2.5 hours a day, six days a week; early crews still lost 2 to 7% bone mineral density depending on site.

sources.title: SANS: 2023 Clinical Update
sources.keyFinding: About 66% of long-duration astronauts show the earliest signs of SANS.

sources.title: Ensuring Astronaut Health (Cardiovascular and Vision Laboratory)
sources.keyFinding: About two liters of fluid shift toward the head in weightlessness, affecting heart, eyes and brain.

sources.title: Increased core body temperature in astronauts during long-duration space missions
sources.keyFinding: Resting core temperature about 1 °C higher in flight, developing over about 2.5 months.

sources.title: Fluid shifts, vasodilatation and ambulatory blood pressure reduction during long duration spaceflight
sources.keyFinding: In eight astronauts on the station, 24-hour average blood pressure was 8 to 10 mmHg lower in flight than before flight (systolic 8, diastolic 9, mean arterial 10 mmHg); the 24-hour average heart rate was unchanged.

sources.title: Spaceflight induces changes in gene expression profiles linked to insulin and estrogen
sources.keyFinding: Insulin resistance has been reported in spaceflight, but studies conflict.

sources.title: 6. Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025
sources.keyFinding: A glucose level below 70 mg/dL is level 1 hypoglycemia, and 70 mg/dL is recognized as the level where people without diabetes start responding to falling glucose; for a conscious person, glucose is the preferred treatment, repeated after 15 minutes if still low.

sources.title: Immune System Dysregulation and Herpesvirus Reactivation Persist During Long-Duration Spaceflight
sources.keyFinding: Varicella-zoster virus reactivated in about half of astronauts on six-month missions.

sources.title: Latent virus reactivation in astronauts on the International Space Station
sources.keyFinding: Reactivation of latent herpes viruses increases on long missions alongside stress hormones.

sources.title: Human Health and Performance (Moon to Mars Architecture)
sources.keyFinding: One-way communication delay to Mars up to 22 minutes; crews need Earth independence.

sources.title: NASA technical report 20170011337 on operations under communication time delay (confirm exact title)
sources.keyFinding: One-way light time to Mars about 182 s at closest and about 1338 s at farthest.

sources.title: Recommendation for a Medical System Concept of Operations for Gateway Missions (NASA HRP-48012)
sources.keyFinding: Gateway missions face an average one-way light-time delay of approximately 1.3 seconds between the Moon and Earth (page 17, section 4.2 Communication).

sources.title: Development of Medical Capabilities and Technologies (decadal topical paper)
sources.keyFinding: Mars delays demand crew medical autonomy and decision support usable by non-medical crew.

sources.title: Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information (DONKI)
sources.keyFinding: Catalog of solar flares, solar energetic particle events and related space weather.

sources.title: Challenge page
sources.keyFinding: Official brief. Its Resources tab must be added to this registry.

sources.title: Anthropometric Measurement Procedures at the Anthropometry and Biomechanics Facility
sources.keyFinding: NASA documents standardized body measurements and uses 3D scanning for human-system design.

sources.title: Bio-Monitor: Keeping an eye on astronauts' vital signs
sources.keyFinding: A wearable system that monitors astronauts' vital signs on the station, including skin temperature.

sources.title: Deltoid, Musculoskeletal Atlas
sources.publisher: University of Washington, Department of Radiology
sources.keyFinding: Reference used to place and label the deltoid area on the outer shoulder.

sources.title: Using Machine Learning Methods to Forecast If Solar Flares Will Be Associated with CMEs and SEPs
sources.publisher: The Astrophysical Journal (arXiv version linked; confirm the journal reference)
sources.keyFinding: Trained support vector machine and neural network classifiers on DONKI flare, CME and SEP associations.

sources.title: Analysis of SEP events and their possible precursors based on the GSEP Catalog
sources.publisher: The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series (arXiv version linked; confirm)
sources.keyFinding: Studies flare magnitude, location and rise time and CME speed and width as SEP predictors, comparing random forest, gradient boosting, logistic regression and support vector machine classifiers.

sources.title: Winners of NASA HRP's Artemis II Data Methodology Challenge
sources.keyFinding: With only four people on board a mission like Artemis II, astronaut health data is limited, and NASA sought methods for such small, high-dimensional datasets.

sources.title: Inspiration4 mission datasets on NASA OSDR (confirm the exact title)
sources.keyFinding: Inspiration4 data covers four civilian astronauts on a three-day mission; the NASA Twins Study covered one astronaut and one ground control.

sources.title: Inspiration4 Mission: Commercial Astronaut Data Now Available on OSDR
sources.keyFinding: Processed Inspiration4 data are public; raw data, including genetic sequence data, need an application with board approval.

sources.title: Why We Do What We Do: Data Reuse, Open Access, and Privacy in Data Management at the Life Sciences Data Archive
sources.keyFinding: The Life Sciences Data Archive protects participants' privacy and consent decisions when it provides human research data for new studies.

sources.title: Ongoing HRP Research in Space
sources.keyFinding: The Human Research Program's overview of its studies now running in space (challenge Resources tab).

sources.title: Monitoring Radiation for Astronaut Health
sources.keyFinding: Radiation is one of the key challenges beyond Earth's protective shield; the CSA is funding a compact, autonomous instrument (CANS) to measure neutron radiation exposure in space, building on earlier radiation detectors used on the station (challenge Resources tab).

sources.title: Why Do We Conduct Science Experiments in Space?
sources.keyFinding: Research on the station aims to understand the health risks of spaceflight and find countermeasures that make space travel safer; Canadian studies cover bones, heart, blood vessels and brain (challenge Resources tab).

sources.title: Early Prediction of Sepsis from Clinical Data: The PhysioNet/Computing in Cardiology Challenge 2019 (dataset, version 1.0.0)
sources.keyFinding: Hourly ICU data for 40,336 patients from two hospital systems with a sepsis label; training and test data of the Earth hospital model.

sources.title: Early Prediction of Sepsis From Clinical Data: The PhysioNet/Computing in Cardiology Challenge 2019
sources.keyFinding: Describes the challenge data and labels, and concludes that generalizing to other hospital systems remains a challenge.
